title_en: Bank of China, Jiangbei Branch v. Agricultural Bank of China, Fandong Branch et al. — dispute over letter of credit advance payment
ruling_gist_en: Where the guarantee contract is invalid due to the invalidity of the main contract, if the guarantor is not at fault, the guarantor shall not bear civil liability; if the guarantor is at fault, the guarantor shall bear civil liability in accordance with the law. The so-called fault of the guarantor refers to circumstances where the guarantor, knowing that the main contract is invalid, nevertheless provides a guarantee for it, or, knowing that the main contract is invalid, nevertheless causes the formation of the main contract or acts as an intermediary for the execution of the main contract.

full_text_en:
Chongqing Jiangbei Sub-branch of Bank of China v. Fandong Sub-branch of Agricultural Bank of China, et al. — dispute over letter of credit advance

[Ruling Summary]

Where a guarantee contract is rendered void due to the invalidity of the underlying principal contract, the guarantor shall bear no civil liability if it is not at fault; if the guarantor is at fault, it shall bear civil liability in accordance with the law. The so-called fault of the guarantor refers to circumstances where the guarantor, with knowledge that the principal contract is void, nevertheless provides a guarantee, or, with knowledge that the principal contract is void, nevertheless facilitates the formation of the principal contract or acts as an intermediary for the execution of the principal contract.

Civil Judgment of the Supreme People's Court

(2003) Min Si Zhong Zi No. 21

Appellant (Plaintiff at First Instance): Chongqing Jiangbei Sub-branch of Bank of China. Domicile: No. 66, Jianxin North Road, Jiangbei District, Chongqing.

Person in Charge: Li Guomo, Branch Manager.

Agent ad litem: Gao Aiguo, lawyer at Beijing Bairui Law Firm.

Appellee (Defendant at First Instance): Fandong Sub-branch of Agricultural Bank of China, Xiangfan City. Domicile: No. 178, Chunyuan Road, Xiangfan City, Hubei Province.

Person in Charge: Liu Hongdong, Branch Manager.

Agent ad litem: Liu Ning, lawyer at Beijing Gongyuan Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Qiao Dong, lawyer at Beijing Gongyuan Law Firm.

Defendant at First Instance: Chongqing Yubei District Foreign Trade Company. Domicile: No. 44, Lane 1, Yuhang Road, Yubei District, Chongqing.

In the case of dispute over letter of credit advance filed by Chongqing Jiangbei Sub-branch of Bank of China (hereinafter referred to as Jiangbei Zhonghang) against Fandong Sub-branch of Agricultural Bank of China, Xiangfan City (hereinafter referred to as Fandong Agricultural Bank) and Chongqing Yubei District Foreign Trade Company (hereinafter referred to as the Foreign Trade Company), the Chongqing High People's Court (hereinafter referred to as the court of first instance) rendered a civil judgment on May 26, 2000, being (1999) Yu Gao Fa Jing Er Chu Zi No. 12. Fandong Agricultural Bank, dissatisfied with the said judgment, filed an appeal to this Court. This Court rendered a civil ruling on November 13, 2001, being (2000) Jing Zhong Zi No. 191, and remanded the case to the court of first instance for retrial on the grounds of unclear facts and insufficient evidence. On August 20, 2003, the court of first instance rendered a civil judgment after retrial, being (2001) Yu Gao Fa Min Chong Zi No. 26. Jiangbei Zhonghang, dissatisfied with the said judgment, filed an appeal to this Court. This Court lawfully formed a collegial panel composed of presiding judge Wang Yun, judge Gao Shawei, and acting judge Chen Jizhong, and held a public hearing of this case on February 10, 2004. The appellant Jiangbei Zhonghang was represented by its agent ad litem Gao Aiguo; the appellee Fandong Agricultural Bank was represented by its person in charge Liu Hongdong and its agents ad litem Liu Ning and Qiao Dong, who appeared in court to participate in the proceedings. The defendant at first instance, the Foreign Trade Company, was lawfully summoned but failed to appear in court without justification. The trial of this case has now been concluded.

The court of first instance found: On March 20, 1997, the Foreign Trade Company entered into Agency Import Agreements No. 97YB-X001, No. 97YB-X002, No. 97YB-X005, No. 97YB-X006, and No. 97YB-X008 with Shanghai Keruide Industrial Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Keruide Company), whereby the parties agreed that the Foreign Trade Company, on behalf of Keruide Company, would import nickel plate and aluminum ingots. On the same day, Fandong Agricultural Bank issued corresponding Irrevocable Guarantees No. 97XFNB-001, No. 97XFNB-002, No. 97XFNB-005, No. 97XFNB-006, and No. 97XFNB-008 to Jiangbei Zhonghang. Under those guarantees, Fandong Agricultural Bank undertook that, upon the Foreign Trade Company's application to Jiangbei Zhonghang for the issuance of letters of credit and the issuance of letters of credit by Jiangbei Zhonghang, and on the premise that the content of the application for issuance of letters of credit submitted by the Foreign Trade Company to Jiangbei Zhonghang was consistent with the content of the agency agreements signed between the Foreign Trade Company and Keruide Company, Fandong Agricultural Bank was willing to provide a guarantee for the Foreign Trade Company, undertaking to bear joint and several liability for all payment, reimbursement, or compensation obligations that the Foreign Trade Company should perform to Jiangbei Zhonghang under the said letters of credit. The scope of the guarantee included the principal, interest, penalty interest, and all related expenses payable by the Foreign Trade Company to Jiangbei Zhonghang under the said letters of credit. Fandong Agricultural Bank also undertook that, as long as the principal amount under the said letters of credit was not increased and the scope of the guarantee was not altered, the guarantee would not be affected or rendered void by any amendment, supplement, deletion, variation in execution of the said letters of credit by the issuing bank, or by any contract entered into between the Foreign Trade Company and other parties. The guarantee would be effective from the date of issuance until the applicant or the guarantor performed all obligations owed to Jiangbei Zhonghang. Fandong Agricultural Bank also undertook that, if any dispute arose as to the interpretation of any wording or provision of the guarantee for whatever reason, the interpretation of the guarantee by the issuing bank would be final and binding on the guarantor.

On March 12, 1997, the Foreign Trade Company applied to Jiangbei Zhonghang for the issuance of an irrevocable letter of credit on the ground of performing the contract for the sale and purchase of aluminum ingots under No. 97YB-I003, with the beneficiary being MARCO INTERNATIONAL (HK) LTD. On March 31 of the same month, Jiangbei Zhonghang issued an irrevocable letter of credit No. 59BIB059/97 for this purpose, with a credit amount of USD 3,990,000. On April 16 of the same year, the Foreign Trade Company issued to Jiangbei Zhonghang a confirmation of payment under the letter of credit, confirming receipt of all documents under the said letter of credit and agreeing to Jiangbei Zhonghang's acceptance and payment. On October 20 of the same year, the Foreign Trade Company applied to Jiangbei Zhonghang for a bill advance, and Jiangbei Zhonghang agreed to an advance for seven days. On October 21 of the same year, Jiangbei Zhonghang made payment and deducted telex charges totaling USD 4,195,546.34.

On April 10, 1997, the Foreign Trade Company applied to Jiangbei Zhonghang for the issuance of an irrevocable letter of credit on the ground of performing the contract for the sale and purchase of nickel plate under No. 97YB-I005, with the beneficiary being GLENWOOD TRADING COMPANY, INC. On April 28 of the same month, Jiangbei Zhonghang issued an irrevocable letter of credit No. 59BIB066/97 for this purpose, with a credit amount of USD 3,600,000. On May 14 of the same year, the Foreign Trade Company issued a confirmation of payment to Jiangbei Zhonghang. On October 23 of the same year, the Foreign Trade Company applied to Jiangbei Zhonghang for a deferral of payment for 181 days. On August 7, 1998, Jiangbei Zhonghang made payment and deducted telex charges totaling USD 3,596,625.

On April 14, 1997, the Foreign Trade Company applied to Jiangbei Zhonghang for the issuance of an irrevocable letter of credit on the ground of performing the contract for the sale and purchase of aluminum ingots under No. 97YB-I006, with the beneficiary being NONFEMET COMMODITY PTE. LTD. On April 30 of the same month, Jiangbei Zhonghang issued an irrevocable letter of credit No. 59BIB072/97 for this purpose, with a credit amount of USD 3,800,000. On May 19 of the same year, the Foreign Trade Company issued a confirmation of payment under the letter of credit to Jiangbei Zhonghang. On October 23 of the same year, the Foreign Trade Company applied to Jiangbei Zhonghang for a deferral of payment for 182 days. On May 18, 1998, Jiangbei Zhonghang made payment and deducted telex charges totaling USD 3,781,475.

On April 15, 1997, the Foreign Trade Company applied to Jiangbei Zhonghang for the issuance of an irrevocable letter of credit on the ground of performing the contract for the sale and purchase of nickel plate under No. 97YB-I007, with the beneficiary being NONFEMET COMMODITY PTE. LTD. On April 29 of the same month, Jiangbei Zhonghang issued an irrevocable letter of credit No. 59BIB076/97 for this purpose, with a credit amount of USD 4,400,000. On May 14 of the same year, the Foreign Trade Company issued a confirmation of payment under the letter of credit to Jiangbei Zhonghang. On May 15, 1998, Jiangbei Zhonghang made payment and deducted telex charges totaling USD 4,464,000.

The total amount of funds advanced by Jiangbei Zhonghang under the above four letters of credit was USD 16,037,646.34. The Foreign Trade Company made two repayments on June 25 and 26, 1998, totaling USD 1,991,000. Therefore, the Foreign Trade Company still owed Jiangbei Zhonghang an advance amount of USD 14,046,646.34.

It was further found: When Jiangbei Zhonghang issued the above four letters of credit, Fandong Agricultural Bank confirmed by telegram the guarantee letters No. 97XFNB-006, No. 97XFNB-008, No. 97XFNB-005, and No. 97XFNB-002, respectively. On April 18, 1997, Fandong Agricultural Bank also sent a letter to Jiangbei Zhonghang, confirming the authenticity of the five Irrevocable Guarantees issued on March 20, 1997, totaling USD 19,700,000, and expressing its willingness to provide a guarantee for the Foreign Trade Company.

On April 14 and May 9, 1997, the Foreign Trade Company respectively sent to Fandong Agricultural Bank "Notifications of Letters of Credit Issued" regarding the above four letters of credit, stating that the Foreign Trade Company, on behalf of Keruide Company, was importing nickel plate or aluminum ingots, and had issued letters of credit through Jiangbei Zhonghang. On the two "Notifications" sent on May 9, the seal of the International Settlement Section of Jiangbei Zhonghang was affixed.

Additionally, during the retrial of this case, Fandong Agricultural Bank submitted that all four letters of credit involved in this case had been subject to bill advances, and provided evidence of the approval procedures for the bill advances. It also claimed that during the hearing at the second instance of the original trial, the agent ad litem for Jiangbei Zhonghang had admitted in court the fact of the bill advances. In response, Jiangbei Zhonghang only admitted the bill advance for letter of credit No. 59BIB059/97 and denied it for the other three letters of credit. Furthermore, Jiangbei Zhonghang submitted to the court of first instance an "Agreement on the Return of Guarantee Letters" to prove that Fandong Agricultural Bank had known about the change in the underlying contract before the letters of credit were issued. However, as the agreement was a photocopy and its content could not prove Jiangbei Zhonghang's claim, the court of first instance did not admit this evidence.

It was further found: According to the industrial and commercial registration materials of the Foreign Trade Company, the company was established on March 12, 1997, with an economic nature of a joint-stock system (shareholding cooperative), with contributors being Chongqing Jiachang Industrial Company (hereinafter referred to as Jiachang Company) and Chongqing Yubei District Foreign Trade Import and Export Company, the legal representative being Chen Fanglun, and registered capital of RMB 30,000,000, of which Jiachang Company contributed RMB 27,000,000.

The audit report No. (1998) 66 issued by Chongqing Dunxin Audit Office (hereinafter referred to as the Audit Report) stated that, upon audit and verification of the letters of credit of Jiachang Company's subsidiary Chongqing Jiachang Metallurgical Company and the Foreign Trade Company, Chongqing Jiachang Metallurgical Company had issued 62 letters of credit from 1995 to 1997, and the Foreign Trade Company had issued 16 letters of credit in 1997 (including the four letters of credit involved in this case), totaling 78 letters of credit. Upon verification, apart from one letter of credit used for agency import, the remaining 77 letters of credit were all used for the purchase and sale of bills of lading for goods abroad. The four letters of credit involved in this case were all for the purchase and sale of bills of lading for goods abroad, and all involved buying at a high price and selling at a low price, with the buyer and seller being the same company. In addition, a review of the flow of funds showed that, as of January 31, 1998, the Foreign Trade Company had received a total of USD 60,915,746.01 in remittances from abroad. As of February 28, 1998, instead of using the proceeds from the transit trade to repay the bank's advances under the letters of credit, the Foreign Trade Company transferred the funds to various units under Jiachang Company and the Chengdu Lhasa Beer Distribution Company, mainly using them to repay the letter of credit advances of Chongqing Jiachang Metallurgical Company, speculate in futures and stocks, etc.

During the retrial in the court of first instance, because it was believed that the four letters of credit involved in this case might involve criminal fraud in letters of credit, and the case of Chen Fanglun, the legal representative of the Foreign Trade Company, suspected of letter of credit fraud, was being supplemented for investigation, the court of first instance issued a civil ruling on August 23, 2002, suspending the trial of this case and simultaneously making a judicial recommendation to the Chongqing Municipal Public Security Bureau. In June 2003, the Economic Investigation Corps of the Chongqing Municipal Public Security Bureau replied: "During the investigation, through the Chongqing Foreign Exchange Administration, it was found that the letters of credit issued by the Foreign Trade Company had been filed. Currently, there is insufficient evidence to prove that a crime was committed." In light of this, the court of first instance promptly resumed the trial of this case.

On September 6, 1999, Jiangbei Zhonghang filed a lawsuit with the court of first instance, requesting that the Foreign Trade Company repay the advance amount under the letters of credit of USD 14,046,646.34 plus interest, penalty interest, and expenses for asserting claims, and that Fandong Agricultural Bank bear joint and several liability.

The court of first instance held: The Foreign Trade Company shall bear liability for repayment of the amounts advanced by Jiangbei Zhonghang under the letters of credit. This case is a dispute over advances under letters of credit arising from an application for the issuance of letters of credit. In the legal relationship of letters of credit, the issuing bank issues a letter of credit upon the application of the applicant, and makes acceptance and payment in accordance with the provisions of the Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credits. After the issuing bank makes advances under the letter of credit in accordance with the provisions of the letter of credit, a creditor-debtor relationship is formed between the applicant and the issuing bank. This legal relationship shall be governed by Article 84, paragraph 2, of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, which provides that "a creditor has the right to demand that the debtor perform its obligations in accordance with the contract or in accordance with the law," and Article 111, which provides that "if one party fails to perform its contractual obligations or performs them in a manner inconsistent with the agreed conditions, the other party has the right to demand performance or to take remedial measures, and has the right to demand compensation for losses." In this case, Jiangbei Zhonghang submitted relevant evidence of the issuance of the letters of credit and the advance of USD 14,046,646.34, while the Foreign Trade Company, after being served with a summons by subpoena, failed to appear in court without justifiable reasons. Therefore, the court found that the fact of the advance claimed by Jiangbei Zhonghang was established, and the Foreign Trade Company should repay the said principal and interest.

Fandong Agricultural Bank shall not bear the guarantee liability under the letters of credit involved in this case. When Fandong Agricultural Bank issued the Irrevocable Guarantees No. 97XFNB-001, No. 002, No. 005, No. 006, and No. 008, it explicitly set out in their preamble a precondition for Fandong Agricultural Bank's undertaking of guarantee liability, namely: on the premise that the content of the application for issuance of letters of credit submitted by the Foreign Trade Company to Jiangbei Zhonghang was consistent with the content of the agency agreements signed between the Foreign Trade Company and Keruide Company, Fandong Agricultural Bank was willing to bear the guarantee liability. Through the trial of this case, there is no evidence to show that Fandong Agricultural Bank waived this precondition for undertaking guarantee liability. Although Fandong Agricultural Bank confirmed the guarantee letters, it only confirmed their authenticity, and did not waive the precondition set at the outset. At the same time, there is no evidence indicating that Fandong Agricultural Bank knew that the application for issuance of letters of credit had altered the trade contract. In fact, the Foreign Trade Company committed fraud against the guarantor, Fandong Agricultural Bank. In the "Notifications of Letters of Credit Issued" dated May 9, 1997, it was still falsely claimed that the letters of credit were issued to import nickel plate and aluminum ingots for Keruide Company. Meanwhile, the affixing of the seal by the International Settlement Section of Jiangbei Zhonghang should be regarded as its knowledge of the fraudulent conduct of the Foreign Trade Company. Pursuant to Article 62 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, which provides that "civil juristic acts may have conditions attached. Conditional civil juristic acts shall become effective when the attached conditions are satisfied," under the circumstances of this case, where the applicant for the issuance of letters of credit changed the underlying trade contract and the guarantor did not explicitly waive the precondition for undertaking guarantee liability, it should be deemed that the attached conditions were not satisfied and the guarantee act is not effective. Moreover, the guarantor is not at fault in this regard. Therefore, Fandong Agricultural Bank shall not bear the guarantee liability in this case.

In summary, the court of first instance, pursuant to Article 62, Article 84, paragraph 2, and Article 111 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, and Article 130 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered the following judgment: 1. The Foreign Trade Company shall, within ten days from the effective date of this judgment, repay to Jiangbei Zhonghang the principal of the advance under the letters of credit of USD 14,046,646.34 and interest (the interest shall be calculated from the date of advance at the interest rate published by the People's Bank of China until full payment); 2. All other claims of Jiangbei Zhonghang are dismissed. The case acceptance fee of RMB 683,823 shall be borne by the Foreign Trade Company. The appeal fee for the second instance of the original trial of RMB 683,823 shall be borne by Jiangbei Zhonghang.

Jiangbei Sub-branch, dissatisfied with the original judgment, appealed to this Court, stating: First, the original judgment contained several major errors and omissions in the findings of fact. (1) The original judgment found that the appellant acknowledged that a trust receipt loan was processed under Letter of Credit No. 59BIB059/97, which is inconsistent with the facts. The Foreign Trade Company did apply for a trust receipt loan, and the appellant agreed to a seven-day trust receipt loan, but in fact the trust receipt loan was not processed, and ultimately the appellant advanced the funds; the Foreign Trade Company did not apply for trust receipt loans for the other three letters of credit. (2) The original judgment's finding that the appellant submitted a copy of an "Agreement on the Return of the Guarantee Letter" was incomplete. The said agreement was an attachment to a reply letter from Fandong Sub-branch to the appellant dated December 28, 1998, and was an agreement between Fandong Sub-branch and the Foreign Trade Company; the appellant could not have had the original. (3) The "Audit Report" cited in the original judgment stated that between 1995 and 1997, Jialong Company's subsidiary, Chongqing Jialong Metallurgy Company, opened 62 letters of credit, and the Foreign Trade Company opened 16 letters of credit in 1997 (including the four letters of credit involved in this case), totaling 78 letters of credit. It should be noted that these two companies had applied to open 106 letters of credit since 1994 at Bank of China Chongqing Branch and Jiangbei Sub-branch, Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, and China Construction Bank, of which 88 had been repaid. Further, it is understood that among those 106 letters of credit, 56 were alleged by the procuratorate to involve crimes. According to a reply to a judicial recommendation letter from the Economic Investigation Detachment of the Chongqing Municipal Public Security Bureau dated April 28, 2003, the 16 letters of credit opened by the Foreign Trade Company were not included in the indictment. (4) The original judgment found that of the 78 letters of credit, apart from one used for agency import, the remaining 77 were all for the purchase and sale of bills of lading for goods abroad, and the four letters of credit involved in this case were all for the purchase and sale of foreign goods bills of lading, all at high purchase prices and low sale prices, with the buyer and seller being the same company. It should be noted that the "Audit Report" states that among the 106 letters of credit, 29 were for ordinary imports and 77 were for entrepot trade. Of the Foreign Trade Company's 16 letters of credit, for four letters of credit the buyer and seller were not the same company, and for Letter of Credit No. 59BIB066/97 involved in this case, the buyer and seller were also not the same company. Although the Foreign Trade Company may have been buying high and selling low, the foreign exchange receipts under the letters of credit indicate that the Foreign Trade Company was buying low and selling high, with each transaction yielding a profit. (5) The original judgment found that as of January 31, 1998, the Foreign Trade Company had received a total of USD 60,915,746.01 from overseas remittances, but these funds were not used to repay the bank's advances under the letters of credit. Instead, by February 28, 1998, the funds were transferred to various units under Jialong Company and to Chengdu Lasa Beer Supply and Sales Company to repay the letter of credit advances of Chongqing Jialong Metallurgy Company, and were used for speculation in futures and stocks, etc. It should be noted that as of February 28, 1998, the advances under the four letters of credit in this case had not yet occurred. Therefore, as of that date, it was impossible to use the proceeds of the entrepot trade to repay the advances under these four letters of credit. Part of the funds from these four letters of credit went to Jialong Company, and part went to Keruide Company (see Appendix 23-4 to the "Audit Report"). (6) On May 9, 1997, the Foreign Trade Company notified the appellant that Letter of Credit No. 59BIB059/97, which had originally been filed with the State Administration of Foreign Exchange for general trade import, was to be changed to entrepot trade import filing.

Second, the original judgment's finding that "where the applicant for the letter of credit changes the underlying trade contract and the guarantor has not expressly waived the conditions for assuming guarantee liability, the conditions should be deemed not fulfilled, and the guarantee act is not effective. Moreover, the guarantor is not at fault for this" is erroneous. (1) Since the guarantee set the precondition that the contents of the letter of credit application must be consistent with the contents of the "agency import agreement," both the guarantor and the issuing bank had the obligation to review this. Once the letter of credit was issued, regardless of subsequent changes in facts, as long as the documents were compliant, the issuing bank was bound to make payment abroad. As long as the Foreign Trade Company did not repay, regardless of whether the trade method changed or whether the actual trade existed, the issuing bank would inevitably advance the funds. Any claims made by the guarantor or the issuing bank after the letter of credit was issued had no effect on the loss from the letter of credit advance and should not change the allocation of responsibility among the parties to the letter of credit. (2) If the guarantor believed that the contents of the letter of credit application were inconsistent with the agency import agreement, it had the obligation to raise this at the time of guarantee verification, and the guarantor is clearly at fault in this regard. (3) Although the guarantee in this case set preconditions, Article 8 of the guarantee letter promised: "The guarantor agrees that, if any ambiguity arises in the understanding of any wording or clause of this guarantee letter for any reason, your bank's interpretation of this guarantee letter shall be final and binding on the guarantor." Therefore, the appellant's understanding and interpretation of the preconditions set in the guarantee letter should also be binding on the guarantor. (4) The preconditions set in the guarantee letter only require that the contents of the letter of credit application be consistent with the contents of the agency import agreement. This cannot be arbitrarily interpreted as requiring that the trade facts after the issuance of the letter of credit be consistent with the agency import agreement. The appellant's obligation to review "consistency" was limited to a facial review of the two documents, namely the letter of credit application and the agency import agreement, before the issuance of the letter of credit. (5) The appellant believed that the letter of credit application was not in conflict with the agency import agreement. The guarantor's guarantee and the act of confirming the guarantee verification were the reasons why the application for the letter of credit was accepted. Once the letter of credit was issued, the guarantor's liability arose. Unless the appellant expressly waived it in writing, the guarantor should bear the guarantee liability.

Third, the original judgment's finding that the appellant's affixing of its seal on the "Notification of Issued Letters of Credit" issued by the Foreign Trade Company on May 9, 1997 constituted knowledge of the Foreign Trade Company's fraudulent conduct was erroneous. First, the four letters of credit involved in this case were issued between March 31 and April 30, 1997. Any subsequent "fraud" by the Foreign Trade Company against Fandong Sub-branch would have been meaningless. Second, in the said notification, the Foreign Trade Company stated that "import" referred to the fact that the letters of credit required for the import stage of the entrepot trade had already been issued, and there was no intention to fabricate facts to defraud. The filing of the Foreign Trade Company's trade method was carried out by the State Administration of Foreign Exchange, and the appellant had no obligation to review its trade method filing. The affixing of the seal was merely a confirmation of the truthfulness of the various key points of issuance relevant to the issuing bank, and did not constitute knowledge of "the Foreign Trade Company's fraudulent conduct." Third, if Fandong Sub-branch believed that the Foreign Trade Company had defrauded it, it should not have entered into the "Agreement on the Return of the Guarantee Letter" with the Foreign Trade Company on July 18, 1997, because that agreement already clarified that "the Foreign Trade Company accepted the entrustment of Keruide Company in March 1997 to act as agent for import or entrepot trade of relevant commodities..." Finally, once the letter of credit was issued, as long as the documents were compliant, the appellant's payment abroad was inevitable, and correspondingly, the guarantor's guarantee liability was also inevitable. The contents of the notification had no effect on the occurrence of the advance. If the Foreign Trade Company had notified Fandong Sub-branch of "agency entrepot trade," or even "loss of goods," the same result of a letter of credit advance would have occurred. Request: 1. To amend the judgment in accordance with the law, ordering Fandong Sub-branch to bear joint and several guarantee liability for the principal of the letter of credit advances owed by the Foreign Trade Company, amounting to USD 14,046,646.34, and the interest; 2. To order Fandong Sub-branch to bear all litigation costs of this case and other costs of realizing the claim.

Fandong Sub-branch did not submit a written defense. At the second-instance trial, Fandong Sub-branch stated: First, the original judgment had clear findings of fact, sufficient evidence, and accurate application of law. Second, the original judgment did not contain the "major errors and omissions" alleged by the appellant. (1) According to the evidence material retrieved by the original trial court from the appellant's letter of credit files, the appellant processed the trust receipt procedures for Letter of Credit No. 59BIB059/97 on October 24, 1997; processed the trust receipt procedures for Letters of Credit No. 72 and No. 76 on May 18, 1998; and processed the trust receipt procedures for Letter of Credit No. 66 on August 7, 1998. The above facts were admitted by the appellant's original agent at the original second-instance trial. Moreover, the "Audit Report" clearly states that "as of August 15, 1998, the above-mentioned unrepaid letters of credit were all overdue, and the bank advanced funds or processed trust receipts..." This wording sufficiently indicates that all four letters of credit in this case had been subjected to trust receipt processing. Therefore, without obtaining our bank's consent, the Foreign Trade Company and the appellant entered into a trust receipt agreement privately, which significantly changed the original contract of issuance and increased the risk to the guarantor. Pursuant to Article 24 of the Guarantee Law of the PRC, our bank should be exempted from guarantee liability. (2) The "Agreement on the Return of the Guarantee Letter" was evidence submitted by the appellant to the original trial court to show that our bank had prior knowledge that the import trade under the four letters of credit in this case had been changed to entrepot trade. However, the appellant was unable to submit the original of this evidentiary material within the time limit for evidence submission set by the original trial court. Therefore, the appellant should bear the consequences of failing to provide evidence. (3) The appellant's statement in ground one, item three of its grounds for appeal, citing the facts found by the original judgment, does not contradict the situation the appellant seeks to clarify. The finding of fact concerns the total of 16 letters of credit opened by the Foreign Trade Company in 1997, which includes the four letters of credit involved in this case. The other circumstances and figures are not legally relevant to this case. (4) Regarding the appellant's grounds one, items four, five, and six, our bank believes the expressions are unclear and the arguments vague, and they cannot support the appellant's requests on appeal.

Third, when our bank issued the guarantee letter, we set preconditions for assuming guarantee liability. If the conditions were fulfilled, the guarantee act would have legal effect; if the conditions were not fulfilled, our bank would have no liability. Therefore, our bank had no need and no legal obligation to review the letter of credit application.

Fourth, the Foreign Trade Company and the appellant had a fraudulent intent subjectively and engaged in fraudulent conduct objectively. (1) Pursuant to the relevant provisions of the Bank of China's "Basic Rules for International Settlement Business," letters of credit must specify the place of shipment and port of destination. In this case, the appellant knew that the Foreign Trade Company's four letter of credit applications were for warehouse receipt futures trading, with neither a place of shipment nor a port of destination, and with an express instruction that the goods could not be transshipped. Nevertheless, the appellant still opened the four letters of credit for futures transactions. The subjective intent is obvious. (2) Our bank provided written confirmation of the authenticity of the guarantee letters on April 1, April 15, and April 18, 1997, respectively, without knowing the true circumstances. (3) After the four letters of credit were issued, the Foreign Trade Company sent "Notifications of Issued Letters of Credit" to our bank on April 14, 1997, and May 9, 1997, respectively. These notifications expressly informed our bank that the Foreign Trade Company, entrusted by Keruide Company, was importing nickel plate and aluminum ingot and had opened letters of credit through Jiangbei Sub-branch. The appellant affixed the official seal of the International Settlement Section on two of the notifications. (4) The facts that have been established by the public security and procuratorial authorities, together with the abnormal circumstances of the four letters of credit in this case being bought high and sold low, confirm that the Foreign Trade Company and the appellant conspired to defraud the guarantee. They opened letters of credit with no underlying trade as usance letters of credit for financing, which was used to repay the appellant's previous substantial debts owed by Jialong Company, which had the same legal representative as the Foreign Trade Company. Request: to dismiss the appeal and affirm the original judgment.

The following facts were ascertained upon trial: This Court confirms the facts found in the original judgment. The appellant, Jiangbei Sub-branch, contended on appeal that the facts found in the original judgment contained six errors and omissions, but none of these contentions can be sustained. Regarding the trust receipt issue, the original judgment only found that the appellant agreed to process a trust receipt for Letter of Credit No. 59BIB059/97, but did not find whether other trust receipt procedures were processed, and did not find whether trust receipts were processed for the other three letters of credit. Regarding the "Agreement on the Return of the Guarantee Letter," the appellant has indeed been unable to provide the original to date. Since the appellee, Fandong Sub-branch, does not admit it, it cannot be used as evidence. Regarding the third, fourth, and fifth alleged errors and omissions, the original trial court merely objectively cited the circumstances stated in the "Audit Report." Regarding the sixth alleged error and omission, the manner in which the State Administration of Foreign Exchange filed Letter of Credit No. 59BIB059/97 has no substantive connection with the handling of the dispute in this case.

This Court further finds: The "Audit Report" was prepared by Chongqing Duxin Auditing Firm on August 24, 1998, upon the entrustment of Jiangbei Sub-branch. The parties to this case have no objection to the authenticity of the "Audit Report." On December 18, 1998, the Jiangbei Task Force of the Inspection Group of the Head Office of Bank of China issued the "Report on the Situation of Chongqing Jialong Metallurgy Co., Ltd. and Chongqing Yubei District Foreign Trade Company Suspected of Fraudulently Obtaining Bank Funds and Evading and Arbitraging Foreign Exchange" (hereinafter referred to as the "Situation Report"), which stated that the Foreign Trade Company, under the guise of so-called entrepot trade, used letters of credit without underlying trade to evade and arbitrage foreign exchange.

The original legal representative of the Foreign Trade Company, Chen Fanglun, was sentenced to life imprisonment for the crime of letter of credit fraud.

This Court, upon trial, is of the opinion:

I. Regarding the Application of Law to the Dispute in this Case

This case involves a dispute over application for the issuance of a letter of credit and a guarantee, which falls within the scope of domestic law. It should be handled in accordance with the relevant provisions of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China and the Guarantee Law of the People's Republic of China and its judicial interpretations.

II. Regarding the Legal Relationship of the Application for Issuance of the Letter of Credit in this Case

The Foreign Trade Company did not appeal in this case, and Jiangbei Sub-branch did not raise any objection to the corresponding facts concerning the advances under the letter of credit issuance legal relationship. Therefore, this Court affirms the result of the original judgment that the Foreign Trade Company should repay the principal and interest of the advances under the letters of credit to Jiangbei Sub-branch. However, the original judgment erred in not explicitly ruling on the validity of the legal relationship of the letter of credit issuance but effectively treating it as valid.

According to the audit content of the "Audit Report" and the content of the "Situation Report," the four letters of credit involved in this case were opened without an underlying trade background. The Foreign Trade Company fabricated the import facts and fraudulently opened letters of credit to obtain foreign exchange from the state. Pursuant to Article 58, paragraph (1), item (3) of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, i.e., "a civil act performed by a party through fraud, duress, or exploitation of the other party's urgent need or improper advantage, causing the other party to act contrary to its true intention, is void," the legal relationship of the letter of credit issuance in this case should be deemed void. The original judgment's application of Article 84, paragraph 2 and Article 111 of the General Principles of the Civil Law to handle the legal relationship of the letter of credit issuance constituted an error in the application of law.

III. Regarding the Legal Relationship of the Guarantee in this Case

Pursuant to Article 5 of the Guarantee Law of the People's Republic of China, i.e., "a guarantee contract is an ancillary contract to the principal contract. If the principal contract is void, the guarantee contract shall also be void," since the legal relationship of the letter of credit issuance in this case is void, the legal relationship of the guarantee in this case should also be deemed void. Pursuant to Article 8 of this Court's Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Guarantee Law of the People's Republic of China, i.e., "where a guarantee contract is void due to the principal contract being void, if the guarantor is not at fault, the guarantor shall not bear civil liability; if the guarantor is at fault, the portion of civil liability borne by the guarantor shall not exceed one-third of the amount that the debtor is unable to repay," whether the guarantor in this case, Fandong Sub-branch, should bear civil liability depends on an examination of whether Fandong Sub-branch was at fault. Determining whether the conditions attached to the guarantee contract have been fulfilled presupposes affirming the validity of the guarantee contract. The original judgment erred in applying the law by finding that the guarantee act was ineffective because the conditions attached to the guarantee contract were not fulfilled, and thus concluding that Fandong Sub-branch did not bear guarantee liability.

Regarding the issue of whether Fandong Sub-branch was at fault. In the situation where the principal contract is void, causing the guarantee contract to be void, the guarantor is not a party to the principal contract. The invalidity of the principal contract should not require the guarantor, who is not a party to the principal contract, to bear the consequences of the invalidity. Therefore, the fault of the guarantor should not refer to the guarantor's fault regarding the invalidity of the principal contract. The fault of the guarantor should include: the guarantor knowingly provides a guarantee for a principal contract that is void, or the guarantor knowingly facilitates the formation of a void principal contract or acts as an intermediary for the execution of a void principal contract, etc. In this case, the legal relationship of the letter of credit issuance was void because the Foreign Trade Company defrauded the issuing bank into issuing letters of credit without underlying trade. At the stage of applying for the issuance of the letter of credit, the guarantor, Fandong Sub-branch, had no way of knowing about the illegality of the contract. Therefore, it should be found that Fandong Sub-branch was not at fault. Pursuant to the aforementioned provisions, Fandong Sub-branch shall not bear civil liability.

In summary, the findings of fact in the original judgment are generally clear, but the application of law was erroneous. Pursuant to Article 153, paragraph (1), item (2) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 58, paragraph (1), item (3) and Article 61, paragraph (1) of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 5 of the Guarantee Law of the People's Republic of China, and Article 8 of the Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Guarantee Law of the People's Republic of China, the judgment is as follows:

1. The civil judgment (2001) Yu Gao Fa Min Zhong Zi No. 26 of the Chongqing High People's Court is set aside;

2. Chongqing Yubei District Foreign Trade Company shall pay to Bank of China Chongqing Jiangbei Sub-branch the principal of the advances under the letters of credit, USD 14,046,646.34, and the interest (interest shall be calculated from the date of advance at the interest rate published by the People's Bank of China until the date of full payment);

3. Agricultural Bank of China Xiangfan Fandong Sub-branch shall not bear civil liability in this case;

4. The other claims of Bank of China Chongqing Jiangbei Sub-branch are dismissed.

The first-instance case acceptance fee is RMB 683,823, to be borne equally by Chongqing Yubei District Foreign Trade Company and Bank of China Chongqing Jiangbei Sub-branch, i.e., RMB 341,911.50 each. The second-instance case acceptance fee is RMB 683,823, to be borne by Bank of China Chongqing Jiangbei Sub-branch.

This judgment is final.
